Msg: Over 90% of cyberattacks start with a phishing email. Before you click, pause and verify. Check the sender, inspect links carefully, and be cautious of urgent requests. When in doubt, do not engage; contact IT immediately.

SMISHING is phishing via SMS. You receive a text that looks like it is from your bank, NIMC, FIRS, or a courier asking you to click a link or call a number urgently. Do not click. Do not call the number in the message. Go directly to the organisation's official website instead. When in doubt, contact IT.

Password123 is not a secure password. A strong password is at least 15 characters, mixes uppercase, lowercase, numbers, and symbols, and means nothing to anyone but you. Better still, use a passphrase; a random string of four or more unrelated words.
MFA prompts you did not initiate must always be denied. If you receive an unexpected MFA request, it means someone has your password and is trying to get in. Deny it and contact IT immediately.

Lock your screen every time you leave your desk, even for two minutes. Press Windows + L instantly. An unlocked screen is an open door to your files, email, and systems.

TAILGATING is when an unauthorised person follows closely behind you through a secured door without using their own access card. Every person must badge in independently. If someone cannot badge in, contact Administration immediately. Do not hold the door.

Public Wi-Fi networks can be monitored by attackers. Never access your work email, financial applications, or any system with sensitive information over public Wi-Fi. Use your mobile data instead.

JUICE JACKING. Public USB charging points in airports and hotels can be modified to steal data or install malware the moment you plug in. Use your own charger and a wall socket instead. Never plug into a USB port you do not own.

88% of all data breaches are caused by employee mistakes, meaning nearly nine in ten breaches originate from human behaviour rather than technical system failures. Be Alert. When in doubt, do not engage, contact IT immediately.
One reported email can prevent a major breach. The cost of reporting a suspicious email is a few seconds of your time. The cost of not reporting it could be far greater. When in doubt, report it.
